1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5.background: Named after the Mexican grandmaster Carlos Torre, who beat the former world champion Emanuel Lasker with it; with 2...d5 it is also called the Tartakower Variation. It is rare at the top level but popular with club players for its calm nature and the little theory it demands.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 Ne4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack, Gossip Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 Ne4.strategy: Hits the bishop at once and spares Black the doubled pawns that Bxf6 would bring. The knight takes a strong central square and White must decide what to do with the bishop, but the knight has moved twice in the opening and can itself be challenged. The more challenging reply.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and opens the king's bishop. It is the natural, solid reply and the most common at amateur level, but the f6 knight is now pinned against the queen by the bishop on g5, and the move plays into the quiet set-up White is after.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 g6.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack, Grünfeld Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 g6.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto so the bishop can press on d4 along the long diagonal. Sound but slow: it does nothing about the bishop on g5, which can take on f6 and double Black's pawns, and White keeps the freedom to shape the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3.strategy: Supports d4 and opens the diagonal for the king's bishop. The dark-squared bishop is already outside the pawn chain, so e3 costs White nothing and the Torre set-up can be completed without hurry.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.Nbd2.strategy: Develops the queen's knight before committing a pawn, which makes the e4 advance possible in one step. The price is a looser hold on d4, held for now only by the knight on f3, and a pawn structure that does not yet deter Black from striking at the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.c4.strategy: Challenges d5 at once, with the pin on f6 already in place. White fights for the centre with a pawn instead of the slow Torre build-up and commits to the more principled, theory-heavy game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 before White has finished the set-up and claims queenside space. Black trades solidity for activity: if the centre opens, the d5 pawn can become an isolated target, but Black's pieces then get open lines.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 Nbd7.strategy: Defends the f6 knight, so the bishop on g5 has nothing to win by taking it and the pin loses its sting. Black keeps a compact, flexible structure and the choice of when to strike at d4, at the cost of a slightly passive knight.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 Be7.strategy: Breaks the pin by putting the bishop between the knight and the queen, and prepares castling. Solid, but Black has not yet struck at d4, so White is free to complete the Torre set-up unhindered.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.c3.strategy: Backs up d4 with a second pawn, which makes the centre safe against exchanges and prepares the e4 advance. The cost is that b2 has no defender, so Black's queen can go after it at once.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.Nbd.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.Nbd.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and keeps the c-pawn at home, so b3 and e4 are covered and the queenside structure stays flexible. White allows Black to open the centre at once in return for smooth development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop toward h7 without first supporting d4 with the c-pawn, so Black can open the centre at once. White stays sound but gives up the slow, solid build-up that this set-up is meant to deliver.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.c3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.c3.strategy: Develops the knight to defend f6 and c5 and keeps the e5 square under watch. It is the flexible, solid way to meet the set-up: Black keeps its pieces behind the pawn chain and accepts a slower build-up than with the knight on c6.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.c3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.c3.strategy: Puts the knight on its most active square and adds a second attacker on d4, so the centre stays under pressure. It does not defend f6, but a trade there is harmless, since the queen retakes.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.c3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack, Breyer Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.c3.strategy: Attacks the undefended b2 pawn straight away and makes White react before the set-up is complete. It is sound, but the queen steps out early and White can offer a trade of queens or defend the pawn, so the pressure may lead to little more than a simplified game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.c3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.c3.strategy: Completes the knight development behind the pawn chain and covers e4, ready for the break that gives this set-up its attacking chances. White has a solid centre and a flexible, patient plan, with the pinned knight as a target.
Brings the bishop to the diagonal toward h7 before the knight and supports the e4 break. The move order matters little: the usual Torre set-up arises, with the kingside as White's target.

Gives up the Torre bishop for the knight at once. Black recaptures with the d7 knight and loses nothing, while White has traded its most active piece and the pin on f6 and has no attack to show for it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.c3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.c3.strategy: Places the bishop on the active diagonal toward White's kingside, eyeing h2 and the e5 square, and clears the way for castling. Unlike the bishop on e7 it leaves the f6 knight pinned to the queen, a small price for the more active bishop.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.c3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.c3.strategy: The solid way to break the pin: the bishop stands between the knight and the queen, so the bishop on g5 stops being a threat, and Black can castle at once. The bishop has less scope than on d6, and Black accepts a compact position.

Hits b2, which nothing defends, and forces White to react. But White can cover it with a queen or rook move, and Black's queen has gone out without winning anything while the minor pieces are still at home.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.c3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.c3.strategy: Places the bishop on the diagonal toward h7 and supports the e4 advance, completing the set-up with the bishops on g5 and d3. White aims at the kingside and gets the harmonious, attack-minded position this opening is meant to deliver.
Develops the last minor piece and covers e4 and b3, reaching the standard Torre set-up with c3 already in. White keeps a solid centre and a flexible bishop, and prepares the e4 break.

Keeps the bishop at home, solid but passive: it gives up the diagonal toward h7 and leaves the e4 break without the bishop's support. White runs no risk, but the attacking idea of the Torre set-up is gone.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.Nbd.strategy: Develops and adds a second attacker on d4 before White has strengthened it with the c-pawn. The pressure on the centre stays and Black keeps its options open, at the price of leaving the f6 knight to the protection of the queen and the g-pawn.

Breaks the pin on f6 and prepares castling, a safe development that keeps every central break in hand. Black gives White time to build the full Torre set-up, but the position stays solid and the tension on d4 remains.

Releases the tension in the centre at once. After exd4 White has a firm pawn on d4 and a half-open e-file, Black a half-open c-file; the game turns quiet and level, and Black has given up some of the flexibility of waiting.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.Nbd.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 c5 5.Nbd.strategy: Strengthens d4 with a second pawn and takes b4 away from Black's knight, completing the base of the set-up. White accepts a slower game in return for a sturdy centre and the e4 break as the plan.

Hurries the bishop to the diagonal toward h7, aiming at the kingside and supporting e4, before d4 has a second pawn defender. Black can open the centre at once, and White must show that the faster development is worth the looser centre.

Pins the c6 knight to the king, so for a moment it cannot take on d4. But Black breaks the pin by developing the c8 bishop, and White must then trade the bishop for the knight or retreat: an active-looking detour that costs time.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 Nbd7 5.B.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 Nbd7 5.B.strategy: Puts the bishop on the diagonal toward h7 and supports the e4 advance. White gets the quick, harmonious development this opening is about, with the kingside as the target.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 Nbd7 5.N.strategy: Develops the queen's knight behind the pawns and prepares the e4 break, leaving the bishop's square and the c-pawn's plan open. A flexible way to reach the usual Torre set-up in whichever move order Black chooses.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.e3 Nbd7 5.c.strategy: Builds the pawn centre first, so d4 is firm whatever Black does. The price is that the pawn blocks the knight's natural square, which has to go to d2, and b2 stays without a defender.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.Nbd2 Be7.strategy: Breaks the pin by putting the bishop between the knight and the queen, so the bishop on g5 stops being a threat, and prepares castling. The bishop is a little passive, but the reply is sturdy and standard.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.Nbd2 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once, before White has played e3 or c3, so for the moment only the f3 knight and the queen hold it. Black claims queenside space and the initiative, at the risk of an isolated d5 pawn if the centre opens.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.Nbd2 Nbd7.strategy: Reinforces the f6 knight and takes control of e5 and c5, so taking on f6 would give White nothing. A compact, flexible set-up in which the c8 bishop still has to find a way out.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.Nbd2 Be7 5..strategy: Supports d4 with a second pawn and makes e4 the natural plan, since the knight on d2 already supports that break. White settles for a sturdy, flexible centre and a slow game.

Supports d4 and frees the king's bishop, with the Torre bishop already outside the pawn chain. A restrained choice: White keeps the c-pawn flexible and decides later how to play for the centre, but does not go for an early break.
Fights for d5 with a pawn, the principled central challenge. But a knight on d2 puts less pressure on d5 than one on c3 would, so the pawn commits White to a fight it is not best placed for.
Develops the queen's knight behind the pawns, covering f6 and e5 against White's plan of e4. Black's position is sturdy and the pin is gone, but it is compact: the bishop on c8 is still shut in.

Castles at once, taking the king out of the centre. The bishop on e7 shields the queen from the pin, so the f6 knight is free to move. Solid and flexible, but the queen's knight and the c8 bishop still have to find squares.
Challenges d4 at once. With c3 played the break is less of a threat, but it gains queenside space and keeps White from building at leisure, giving Black active play rather than waiting passively.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.Nbd2 Be7 5..name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 e6 4.Nbd2 Be7 5..strategy: Fills in the pawn structure of the set-up: d4 is backed by two pawns and the king's bishop is free. White follows the same slow, harmonious plan as in the other move orders, with the e4 break to come.

Puts the queen on the diagonal toward h7 and backs the e4 break, the idea behind the whole set-up. The cost is time: the king's bishop is still shut in behind the e-pawn and the king is not yet safe, so Black has a moment to act in the centre.

Gives up the active bishop for the knight. Black recaptures with a piece, so White has no structural damage to show for it and has traded its most active bishop for a defender that is easily replaced. Not a mistake, but it leaves Black comfortable.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 g6 4.e3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack, Grünfeld Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 g6 4.e3.strategy: Supports d4 and opens the king's bishop, a calm start against the fianchetto. The bishop on g5 still threatens to take on f6 and double Black's pawns, which makes Black's set-up less comfortable than it looks.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 g6 4.Nbd2.strategy: Develops the knight without blocking the c-pawn, and from d2 it backs a later e4. The bishop on g5 stays aimed at the knight on f6, so Black's fianchetto set-up never feels entirely free, and White keeps a solid, flexible position.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5 g6 4.Bxf6.strategy: Takes the knight to double Black's f-pawns after ...exf6, but Black gets the two bishops and a half-open e-file for the damaged structure. White gives up its most active piece for an advantage that is hard to turn into anything concrete.
